steps.title: Perfumed and dry
steps.body: Torrontés gives intensely aromatic whites with rose, jasmine, orange blossom, peach, lemon and lychee. Most are dry, with medium acidity and medium to high alcohol, and sometimes a slightly bitter finish. Its perfume makes it seem sweet, but it's usually dry.

steps.title: An Argentine cross
steps.body: There are three Torrontés: Riojano, the finest and most planted, Sanjuanino and Mendocino. DNA shows Torrontés Riojano is a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, also called Listán Prieto or País, brought by Spanish colonists. That explains its Muscat-like perfume. It's Argentina's own grape, born there.
steps.highlight: Muscat of Alexandria x Criolla Chica

steps.prompt: Why does Torrontés smell like Muscat?
options: Muscat of Alexandria is one of its parents
steps.explanation: Its parentage gives it Muscat-like terpenes.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour and an explosive floral nose of rose and orange blossom, then a dry palate with medium acidity and warm alcohol. A slight bitterness at the end is typical. Compared with Muscat, it's often drier and spicier; compared with Gewürztraminer, fresher.

points: Torrontés is intensely floral but usually dry
